meta.title: GRE Core 250
meta.selection: Top words by agreement across published GRE high-frequency lists (weighted); batches ordered by everyday-English frequency, easiest first.

sources.name: PowerScore GRE Vocabulary: Repeat Offenders (700 words PowerScore flags as recurring on the GRE)
Princeton Review 'Hit Parade' (most frequently tested GRE words)

provincial.definition: narrow in outlook; unsophisticated, as if limited to one's own small region
provincial.example: Raised in a remote village, she was embarrassed by her provincial assumptions about city life.

intimate.definition: to hint or suggest indirectly, without saying outright
intimate.example: The senator intimated that he might resign without ever saying so directly.
intimate.note: As a verb it is pronounced IN-tuh-mayt. The GRE tests this "hint" sense, not the "close/private" adjective.

aesthetic.definition: concerned with beauty or the appreciation of beauty
aesthetic.example: The architect cared less about cost than about the building's aesthetic appeal.

rhetoric.definition: the art of persuasive speaking or writing; often, showy language with little real substance
rhetoric.example: The candidate's soaring rhetoric masked the fact that he had no concrete plan.

arbitrary.definition: based on random choice or personal whim rather than reason or a system
arbitrary.example: The dean's decision seemed arbitrary because he never explained his criteria.

obscure.definition: not well known; hard to understand or see clearly (v.: to make unclear or hide)
obscure.example: The poet remained obscure until a critic rediscovered his work decades later.

partisan.definition: strongly (often blindly) supporting one side, party, or cause; biased (n.: such a supporter)
partisan.example: Partisan bickering prevented the committee from agreeing on even a small compromise.

derivative.definition: copied from or based on the work of others; lacking originality
derivative.example: Critics dismissed the film as derivative, a patchwork of scenes borrowed from classic westerns.

empirical.definition: based on observation or experiment rather than on theory alone
empirical.example: The theory is elegant, but it lacks empirical support.

ambiguous.definition: open to more than one interpretation; unclear
ambiguous.example: The contract's wording was ambiguous, and each side claimed it supported them.

discrete.example: The survey sorted answers into three discrete categories with no overlap.
discrete.note: Not the same as discreet (tactful, careful about what you say).

eminent.definition: famous and respected in a particular field; distinguished
eminent.example: An eminent physicist was invited to deliver the keynote address.
eminent.note: Not the same as imminent (about to happen).

mitigate.definition: to make less severe, harmful, or painful
mitigate.example: Planting trees along the river helped mitigate the effects of flooding.

pragmatic.definition: dealing with things sensibly and realistically, based on practical rather than theoretical concerns
pragmatic.example: A pragmatic leader, she accepted a smaller deal rather than risk losing everything.

implicit.definition: implied though not stated outright; also, absolute and unquestioning
implicit.example: There was an implicit threat in his polite reminder about the deadline.

mundane.definition: lacking interest or excitement; dull and ordinary
mundane.example: After the thrill of the expedition, the mundane routine of office life felt stifling.

sanction.definition: v.: to authorize or approve; n.: approval, but also (usually plural) a penalty for breaking a rule
sanction.example: The council refused to sanction the project until its environmental impact was assessed.
sanction.note: A contronym: it can mean "approve" or "punish". Context decides, so watch the sentence.

emulate.definition: to imitate in an effort to equal or surpass
emulate.example: Young writers often emulate the authors they admire most.

prudent.definition: wise and careful in practical matters; cautious about the future
prudent.example: It would be prudent to save part of your income before making such a large purchase.

pervasive.definition: spreading widely through every part of something; present everywhere
pervasive.example: Distrust of the government was so pervasive that even routine announcements were doubted.

eclectic.definition: drawing on a wide range of sources, styles, or ideas
eclectic.example: Her eclectic taste in music ranges from medieval chant to punk rock.

endemic.definition: regularly found in a particular place or among a particular group; native to it
endemic.example: Malaria is endemic to many tropical regions.

opaque.definition: not transparent; hard to understand or interpret
opaque.example: The agency's opaque accounting made it impossible to tell where the money went.

transient.definition: lasting only a short time; temporary (n.: a person who stays briefly)
transient.example: The fame of a viral video star is usually transient.

archaic.definition: belonging to an earlier period; outdated
archaic.example: Words like "thou" and "hath" now sound archaic.

conspicuous.example: Her bright red coat made her conspicuous in the gray crowd.

maverick.definition: an independent-minded person who refuses to follow the conventions of a group
maverick.example: The maverick economist rejected the field's consensus and published a very different forecast.

pristine.definition: in its original, unspoiled, untouched condition; pure
pristine.example: The hikers reached a pristine lake that no road had ever approached.

bolster.example: New evidence from the lab bolstered the researchers' claim.

contentious.definition: causing or likely to cause argument; fond of quarreling
contentious.example: The tax proposal was so contentious that the debate lasted for weeks.

sporadic.example: Sporadic gunfire could be heard through the night, but nothing sustained.

lucid.definition: clearly expressed and easy to understand; also, mentally clear and rational
lucid.example: Her lucid explanation made the complex theory accessible to beginners.

precarious.definition: dangerously unstable or uncertain; dependent on chance
precarious.example: The climber's position on the narrow ledge was precarious.

apathy.definition: lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern
apathy.example: Voter apathy was blamed for the record-low turnout.

disparate.definition: essentially different in kind; so unlike that comparison is hard
disparate.example: The museum displayed disparate objects: a jade carving, a locomotive wheel, and a 1950s radio.

luminous.definition: giving off light; glowing; also, clear and enlightening
luminous.example: The moon was luminous above the dark lake.

meticulous.definition: showing great care and attention to detail
meticulous.example: The restorer was meticulous, cleaning each fragment with a tiny brush.

plethora.example: A plethora of options left the shoppers more confused than before.

appease.definition: to pacify or placate, often by giving in to demands
appease.example: The manager gave the angry customer a refund in an attempt to appease him.

craven.example: The craven guard fled at the first sign of trouble.

arduous.example: The arduous climb took the team nearly nine hours.

esoteric.definition: understood by or meant for only a small group with specialized knowledge
esoteric.example: The professor's lecture on esoteric points of medieval law lost most of the class.

propensity.example: He has a propensity for exaggerating his accomplishments.

refute.definition: to prove a claim or person wrong with argument or evidence
refute.example: The data refuted the hypothesis that the drug was effective.

frugal.example: Growing up in poverty made her frugal for the rest of her life.

copious.example: He took copious notes throughout the lecture.

egregious.definition: outstandingly bad; shocking in a conspicuous way
egregious.example: The editor was appalled by the egregious factual errors in the article.

elicit.definition: to draw out (a response, reaction, or piece of information)
elicit.example: The comedian's joke failed to elicit even a smile.

whimsical.example: The garden's whimsical sculptures included a dancing teapot.

nuance.definition: a subtle difference in meaning, tone, or expression
nuance.example: The translator struggled to preserve every nuance of the poem.

abstain.definition: to deliberately hold oneself back from doing something, especially voting or indulging
abstain.example: He abstained from alcohol throughout his training.

penchant.definition: a strong liking or habitual inclination
penchant.example: She has a penchant for wearing outlandish hats.

innocuous.example: The remark seemed innocuous, but it deeply offended her.

convoluted.definition: extremely complex and difficult to follow; intricately twisted
convoluted.example: The film's convoluted plot required a flowchart to follow.

paragon.definition: a model of excellence or perfection
paragon.example: She was held up as a paragon of integrity.

intrepid.example: The intrepid explorer crossed the desert alone.

disseminate.example: The organization uses social media to disseminate health information.

insular.definition: isolated; narrow-minded and uninterested in outside ideas
insular.example: The insular community distrusted outsiders and their new ideas.

eulogy.definition: a speech or piece of writing praising someone, especially one who has died
eulogy.example: Her son delivered a moving eulogy at the funeral.

fawn.definition: to seek favor by flattery and servile attention (usually "fawn over/on")
fawn.example: Courtiers fawned over the king, praising even his worst jokes.
fawn.note: Here it is a verb, not the baby deer.

ambivalent.definition: having mixed or contradictory feelings about something
ambivalent.example: She felt ambivalent about leaving, both eager and afraid.
ambivalent.note: Not "indifferent": the person feels strongly in two directions.

austere.definition: severe or strict in manner; plain and without luxury
austere.example: The monks lived an austere life in bare stone cells.

superfluous.example: Cut every superfluous word from your essay.

arcane.example: The legal code was full of arcane rules that only specialists could decipher.

ephemeral.example: The beauty of cherry blossoms is ephemeral; they fall within days.

caustic.definition: sarcastic and bitingly critical; able to corrode
caustic.example: The reviewer's caustic wit spared no one in the cast.

deference.definition: respectful submission to the judgment or wishes of another
deference.example: Out of deference to his elders, he stayed silent.

spurious.definition: not genuine; false though appearing authentic
spurious.example: The historian exposed the diary as a spurious document.

audacious.definition: bold and daring, sometimes insolently so
audacious.example: The audacious plan to cross the ocean on a raft shocked everyone.

disingenuous.definition: not candid or sincere; pretending to know less than one does
disingenuous.example: It was disingenuous of her to claim surprise at a decision she herself had made.

anomalous.definition: deviating from what is normal or expected
anomalous.example: The anomalous results suggested a flaw in the experiment.

censure.definition: strong, formal disapproval; to criticize harshly
censure.example: The senator was censured by his colleagues for misusing campaign funds.

reproach.definition: to express disapproval or disappointment; blame
reproach.example: She reproached her son for forgetting his promise.

tacit.definition: understood or implied without being stated
tacit.example: Silence on the matter was taken as tacit agreement.

veracity.example: The journalist checked the veracity of every claim.

dogmatic.definition: asserting opinions as undeniable truth; inflexible in belief
dogmatic.example: His dogmatic insistence that he alone was right ended the discussion.

corroborate.definition: to confirm or support with additional evidence
corroborate.example: Two independent witnesses corroborated her account.

euphemism.definition: a mild or indirect word used in place of one considered too harsh or blunt
euphemism.example: "Passed away" is a common euphemism for "died."

exacerbate.definition: to make a problem or bad situation worse
exacerbate.example: Scratching the rash only exacerbated the irritation.

malevolent.definition: having or showing a wish to do evil to others
malevolent.example: The villain cast a malevolent glare at the hero.

onerous.example: The new regulations imposed onerous paperwork on small businesses.

prodigal.definition: spending money recklessly and wastefully; lavish (n.: a wasteful spender)
prodigal.example: The prodigal heir squandered his fortune within a decade.
prodigal.note: Easily confused with prodigious (huge). Prodigal = wasteful.

prodigious.definition: remarkably great in size, extent, or degree
prodigious.example: Mozart displayed a prodigious talent from early childhood.

disinterested.definition: impartial; having no personal stake in the outcome
disinterested.example: We need a disinterested judge who has no financial stake in the outcome.
disinterested.note: Not the same as uninterested (bored, not caring). The GRE tests exactly this distinction.

amenable.definition: open and responsive to suggestion or persuasion; cooperative
amenable.example: The board was amenable to revising the schedule.

banal.definition: so lacking in originality as to be boring; trite
banal.example: The film's banal dialogue could have come from a thousand other movies.

decorum.example: The judge demanded decorum in the courtroom.

pernicious.definition: harmful in a gradual or subtle way
pernicious.example: The pernicious rumor slowly eroded the company's reputation.

rescind.definition: to revoke, cancel, or repeal officially
rescind.example: The university rescinded the offer after discovering the false claims on his application.

tirade.example: The coach launched into a tirade against the referee.

presumptuous.definition: failing to observe the limits of what is appropriate; overly bold or confident
presumptuous.example: It was presumptuous of the intern to rewrite the director's speech.

immutable.definition: unchanging over time; unable to be changed
immutable.example: Newton believed the laws of nature were immutable.

commensurate.definition: corresponding in size, amount, or degree; proportionate
commensurate.example: The salary offered was commensurate with her experience.

itinerant.definition: traveling from place to place, especially for work
itinerant.example: The itinerant preacher moved from town to town.

malleable.example: Gold is malleable enough to be hammered into thin sheets.

mercurial.definition: subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood
mercurial.example: The mercurial director could be charming at breakfast and furious by lunch.

ascetic.definition: practicing severe self-discipline and avoiding indulgence (n.: such a person)
ascetic.example: He led an ascetic life, eating only bread and water.

capricious.definition: given to sudden, unpredictable changes of mind or behavior
capricious.example: The capricious king banished a minister one day and rewarded him the next.

extraneous.definition: irrelevant or unrelated to the subject; not essential
extraneous.example: Delete the extraneous details so the summary stays focused.

propriety.definition: conformity to accepted standards of behavior or morals
propriety.example: She was careful to observe the proprieties at the formal dinner.

dupe.definition: to deceive or trick (n.: a person who is easily tricked)
dupe.example: The con artist duped hundreds of investors.

precipitate.definition: v.: to cause something to happen suddenly or too soon; adj.: done hastily, rash
precipitate.example: The scandal precipitated the minister's resignation.

placate.definition: to calm or soothe someone's anger
placate.example: A sincere apology placated the angry customer.

conciliatory.definition: intended to calm anger or end a dispute
conciliatory.example: The CEO adopted a conciliatory tone to defuse the dispute.

erudite.example: The erudite professor quoted Latin as casually as most people quote movies.

didactic.definition: intended to teach, often in an overly moralizing way
didactic.example: The novel was so didactic that readers felt they were being lectured.

obstinate.definition: stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action
obstinate.example: The obstinate mule would not budge despite the farmer's coaxing.

petulant.example: The petulant child threw his toys when told it was bedtime.

deleterious.example: Prolonged lack of sleep has a deleterious effect on memory.

cogent.example: She presented a cogent argument that won over the skeptics.

gregarious.example: The gregarious host made sure every guest felt welcome.

antipathy.example: There was a long-standing antipathy between the two rival families.

elucidate.example: The professor used diagrams to elucidate the difficult concept.

aberrant.definition: departing from the usual or expected course
aberrant.example: The patient's aberrant behavior puzzled the doctors.

anachronistic.definition: belonging to a time other than the one in which it appears; out of date
anachronistic.example: A wristwatch in a film about ancient Rome would be glaringly anachronistic.

incongruous.definition: out of place; not in harmony with its surroundings
incongruous.example: A neon sign looked incongruous against the medieval stonework.

proliferate.example: Coffee shops have proliferated in the neighborhood.

fortuitous.definition: happening by chance, especially by lucky chance
fortuitous.example: Their meeting was entirely fortuitous; neither had planned to attend.
fortuitous.note: Strictly means "by chance", not "fortunate", though it is often lucky.

ostentatious.definition: showy; designed to impress or attract notice
ostentatious.example: The oligarch's ostentatious mansion had gold-plated faucets.

panache.definition: flamboyant confidence of style or manner
panache.example: She delivered the speech with panache.

pedantic.definition: excessively concerned with minor details or rules, or showing off learning
pedantic.example: His pedantic insistence on correcting everyone's grammar annoyed his friends.

confound.definition: to confuse or astonish; also, to prove wrong
confound.example: The results confounded the researchers' expectations.

tortuous.definition: full of twists and turns; excessively complicated
tortuous.example: The tortuous mountain road made her carsick.
tortuous.note: Not torturous (causing torture or great pain).

fallacious.definition: based on a mistaken belief or faulty reasoning
fallacious.example: The argument is fallacious because it assumes what it is trying to prove.

fastidious.definition: very attentive to detail; hard to please
fastidious.example: He was so fastidious about cleanliness that he wiped each fork twice.

glib.example: The salesman's glib assurances did not convince her.

insipid.example: The soup was thin and insipid, as was the conversation.

myopic.definition: short-sighted, literally or in lacking foresight
myopic.example: The myopic policy solved this year's deficit but ignored long-term costs.

assuage.definition: to make (pain, fear, anger) less intense
assuage.example: A warm bath assuaged her aching muscles.

bombastic.definition: high-sounding but with little meaning; pompous
bombastic.example: The senator's bombastic speech was full of grand phrases and empty of ideas.

coalesce.definition: to come together to form one mass or whole
coalesce.example: Scattered protests coalesced into a nationwide movement.

engender.definition: to cause or give rise to (a feeling or situation)
engender.example: Unfair treatment engenders resentment among employees.

reticent.definition: reluctant to speak or share thoughts; reserved
reticent.example: He was reticent about his past and never mentioned his family.

exonerate.definition: to clear of blame or accusation
exonerate.example: DNA evidence exonerated the man after twenty years in prison.

implacable.definition: unable to be appeased or pacified; relentless
implacable.example: The implacable critic refused to praise even the finest performance.

magnanimous.definition: generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful
magnanimous.example: The magnanimous champion praised the opponent he had just defeated.

paucity.definition: scarcity; a smallness of number or quantity
paucity.example: A paucity of evidence forced the prosecutors to drop the case.

laud.example: Critics lauded the novel as a masterpiece.

levity.definition: humor or lack of seriousness, especially at an inappropriate time
levity.example: A moment of levity eased the tension in the meeting.

denigrate.example: She never denigrated her rivals, preferring to let her work speak for itself.

diatribe.example: His diatribe against the new policy lasted nearly an hour.

disparage.definition: to speak of as being of little value; belittle
disparage.example: It is unprofessional to disparage a colleague's work in front of clients.

eschew.definition: to deliberately avoid or abstain from
eschew.example: She eschews fast food and cooks every meal from scratch.

scrupulous.definition: extremely careful and thorough; strictly honest
scrupulous.example: The accountant was scrupulous in recording every transaction.

ameliorate.definition: to make a bad situation better
ameliorate.example: Government aid did little to ameliorate the plight of the displaced.

delineate.definition: to describe or portray precisely; to outline
delineate.example: The report delineates each department's responsibilities.

supplant.definition: to replace, especially by force or by being superior
supplant.example: Digital cameras supplanted film in less than a decade.

efficacious.definition: successful in producing the desired result; effective
efficacious.example: Aspirin is efficacious for relieving mild pain.

recalcitrant.definition: stubbornly resistant to authority or control
recalcitrant.example: The recalcitrant student refused to follow even the simplest rules.

languid.definition: lacking energy or vitality; slow and relaxed
languid.example: In the heat, we spent a languid afternoon in hammocks.

predilection.definition: a preference or special liking for something
predilection.example: She has a predilection for mystery novels.

facetious.definition: treating serious matters with inappropriate humor; flippant
facetious.example: I was being facetious when I suggested we cancel the exam; of course we can't.

avarice.example: The miser's avarice drove him to count every penny twice.

furtive.example: He cast a furtive glance at his neighbor's answer sheet.

polemical.definition: involving or given to strong controversial argument
polemical.example: The essay was a polemical attack on the education system.

contrite.definition: feeling or expressing remorse for wrongdoing
contrite.example: The contrite boy promised never to lie again.

relegate.definition: to assign to a lower or less important position
relegate.example: Budget cuts relegated the arts program to an afterthought.

circumspect.definition: cautious; careful to consider all circumstances and consequences
circumspect.example: Given the political tension, the diplomat was circumspect in her remarks.

reverent.example: The pilgrims entered the shrine in reverent silence.

belie.definition: to contradict or give a false impression of
belie.example: His calm tone belied the anger he felt.

perfunctory.definition: done routinely with minimal effort or interest
perfunctory.example: The inspector gave the building a perfunctory glance and signed off.

repudiate.definition: to refuse to accept or be associated with; to reject as untrue
repudiate.example: The candidate repudiated the extremist views of his supporter.

specious.definition: seemingly plausible but actually false or flawed
specious.example: The lawyer's specious argument sounded convincing but collapsed under scrutiny.

vociferous.example: The mayor faced vociferous opposition at the town meeting.

bucolic.definition: relating to pleasant rural or pastoral life
bucolic.example: The painting shows a bucolic scene of shepherds and meadows.

morose.example: He sat in morose silence after losing his job.

verbose.example: The verbose report could have been shortened to two pages.

deride.definition: to ridicule; to speak of with contempt
deride.example: Skeptics derided the inventor's plan as absurd.

foment.definition: to stir up or incite (trouble, rebellion)
foment.example: Agitators fomented unrest among the workers.

hackneyed.example: "Love at first sight" is a hackneyed plot device.

laconic.example: His laconic reply, "Fine," told her nothing.

probity.definition: strong moral principles; honesty and integrity
probity.example: The judge was known for his probity.

dirge.definition: a slow, mournful song or lament
dirge.example: The band played a dirge as the procession passed.

profligate.definition: recklessly extravagant or wasteful (n.: a wasteful person)
profligate.example: The profligate duke gambled away the family estate.

restive.definition: unable to stay still or be controlled; restless
restive.example: The restive crowd began to shout when the speaker was late.

taciturn.example: The taciturn farmer answered most questions with a nod.

torpor.definition: a state of physical or mental inactivity; sluggishness
torpor.example: After the huge meal, a pleasant torpor settled over the guests.

abeyance.definition: a state of temporary inactivity or suspension
abeyance.example: The plan was held in abeyance until funding was approved.

alacrity.example: She accepted the invitation with alacrity.

attenuate.definition: to reduce in force, effect, or value; to make thinner

germane.definition: relevant to the subject at hand
germane.example: Please keep your comments germane to the topic of today's meeting.

approbation.example: The play won the approbation of the critics.

admonish.definition: to warn or reprimand gently but firmly
admonish.example: The teacher admonished the class to stop talking.

intransigent.definition: unwilling to change one's views or compromise
intransigent.example: The two sides remained intransigent, and the talks collapsed.

irascible.example: The irascible old man yelled at anyone who stepped on his lawn.

dilettante.definition: a person who dabbles in a subject without serious commitment
dilettante.example: A mere dilettante, he took up painting, then sculpture, then gave up both.

venerate.definition: to regard with great respect and reverence

indolent.example: The indolent student did the minimum and slept through lectures.

chicanery.definition: the use of trickery or deception to achieve a goal
chicanery.example: The firm won the contract through legal chicanery.

amalgamate.definition: to combine or unite into one organization or structure
amalgamate.example: The two banks amalgamated to form a larger institution.

fatuous.definition: silly and pointless, showing a lack of thought
fatuous.example: She dismissed the fatuous remark with a sigh.

quotidian.definition: of or occurring every day; ordinary
quotidian.example: The novel finds poetry in quotidian routines like making breakfast.

surfeit.example: A surfeit of rich food left him feeling ill.

tractable.definition: easy to control or influence; docile
tractable.example: Unlike the stubborn horse, this one is gentle and tractable.

aver.definition: to state or assert confidently as a fact
aver.example: The witness averred that she had never seen the defendant.
aver.note: Not the same as avert (to turn away or prevent).

misanthrope.definition: a person who dislikes and avoids other people
misanthrope.example: The misanthrope lived alone and rarely left his house.

sycophant.definition: a person who flatters the powerful to gain advantage
sycophant.example: The king was surrounded by sycophants who agreed with everything he said.

parsimonious.definition: extremely unwilling to spend money; stingy
parsimonious.example: The parsimonious uncle reused tea bags three times.

ebullient.definition: cheerful and full of energy; exuberant
ebullient.example: She was ebullient after winning the scholarship.

inimical.example: Policies inimical to small business will hurt the local economy.

platitude.definition: a trite remark presented as if it were meaningful
platitude.example: The speech was a string of platitudes about hard work.

iconoclast.definition: a person who attacks cherished beliefs or institutions
iconoclast.example: An iconoclast, he mocked the sacred traditions of the profession.

obsequious.definition: excessively eager to please or obey; fawning
obsequious.example: The obsequious waiter bowed at every request.

salubrious.example: The doctor recommended a stay in the salubrious mountain air.

garrulous.definition: excessively talkative, especially about trivial matters
garrulous.example: The garrulous neighbor talked for an hour about her cat.

loquacious.definition: tending to talk a great deal
loquacious.example: After a coffee or two, he became loquacious.

obviate.definition: to make unnecessary; to prevent or remove (a difficulty) in advance
obviate.example: The new software obviates the need for manual data entry.

opprobrium.definition: harsh public criticism or disgrace arising from shameful conduct
opprobrium.example: The company faced public opprobrium after the scandal.

desultory.definition: lacking a plan or purpose; jumping from one thing to another
desultory.example: They made desultory conversation while waiting for the train.

diffident.definition: modest or shy because of a lack of self-confidence
diffident.example: The diffident young scholar hesitated to share his ideas.

soporific.definition: tending to induce drowsiness or sleep (n.: a sleep-inducing drug)
soporific.example: The lecture was so soporific that half the audience dozed.

penury.example: After the business failed, he lived in penury.

perfidious.definition: deceitful and untrustworthy; guilty of betrayal
perfidious.example: The perfidious ally secretly signed a treaty with the enemy.

officious.definition: assertive in offering unwanted help or authority; meddlesome
officious.example: An officious clerk insisted on checking forms that no one had asked him to check.

abscond.definition: to leave hurriedly and secretly, typically to avoid arrest or to take something
abscond.example: The cashier absconded with the day's receipts.

harangue.definition: a lengthy, aggressive, ranting speech; to lecture at length in that manner
harangue.example: The coach harangued his players for an hour after the loss.

inundate.definition: to flood; to overwhelm with a large quantity
inundate.example: After the broadcast, the station was inundated with calls.

phlegmatic.example: The phlegmatic captain showed no fear as the storm approached.

inchoate.definition: only partly formed; just beginning, undeveloped
inchoate.example: Her ideas were still inchoate and needed more work.

mendacious.example: The mendacious witness was caught in a web of contradictions.

burnish.definition: to polish by rubbing; to improve (a reputation or image)
burnish.example: The mayor tried to burnish his image with a charity campaign.

mollify.definition: to soothe the anger or anxiety of
mollify.example: The waiter offered free dessert to mollify the disgruntled diners.

disabuse.definition: to free someone from a mistaken belief
disabuse.example: Let me disabuse you of the notion that the exam will be easy.

obdurate.definition: stubbornly refusing to change one's mind or course of action
obdurate.example: The obdurate chairman ignored every plea to reconsider.

stolid.definition: calm, dependable, showing little emotion or excitement
stolid.example: The stolid guard did not flinch at the insults.

truculent.definition: eager or quick to argue or fight; defiantly aggressive
truculent.example: The truculent customer slammed the counter and demanded a manager.

calumny.definition: a false statement made to damage someone's reputation
calumny.example: He sued the newspaper over its calumny against him.

idiosyncrasy.definition: a peculiar habit or characteristic specific to an individual
idiosyncrasy.example: One of his idiosyncrasies was refusing to eat anything green.

effrontery.example: She had the effrontery to ask for a raise on her first day.

castigate.example: The coach castigated the team for their lack of effort.

ingenuous.example: His ingenuous questions revealed that he knew nothing of the city's politics.
ingenuous.note: Opposite of disingenuous. Not the same as ingenious (clever).

imperturbable.definition: unable to be upset or excited; calm
imperturbable.example: The imperturbable pilot calmly steered the plane through turbulence.

dissemble.definition: to hide one's true feelings or intentions; to disguise
dissemble.example: She dissembled her fear behind a polite smile.
dissemble.note: Not the same as disassemble (take apart).

dilatory.definition: slow to act; intended to delay
dilatory.example: The dilatory clerk took weeks to process a simple form.

abjure.definition: to solemnly renounce or reject (a belief or claim)
abjure.example: He abjured violence and became a pacifist.

occlude.example: A blood clot occluded the artery.

demur.definition: to raise objections or show reluctance
demur.example: When asked to work on Sunday, he demurred.

vacillate.definition: to waver between different opinions or actions
vacillate.example: She vacillated between accepting the job and staying put.

munificent.definition: very generous; larger or more generous than usual
munificent.example: A munificent donor funded the new library.

recondite.definition: little known; dealing with profound or obscure subject matter
recondite.example: The treatise was so recondite that only a handful of scholars could read it.

equivocate.definition: to use ambiguous language so as to avoid commitment or conceal the truth
equivocate.example: Pressed on the tax rise, the minister equivocated.

burgeon.definition: to grow or increase rapidly; flourish
burgeon.example: The city's tech sector burgeoned in the 2010s.

exculpate.definition: to show or declare that someone is not guilty

prevaricate.definition: to speak or act evasively; to stretch the truth
prevaricate.example: Rather than admit his error, he prevaricated.

gainsay.example: No one could gainsay the accuracy of her statistics.

propitiate.definition: to win or regain the favor of (an angry person or god) by doing something pleasing
propitiate.example: Ancient farmers offered sacrifices to propitiate the gods of the harvest.

upbraid.example: The manager upbraided the intern for missing the deadline.

desiccate.definition: to remove moisture from; to dry out completely
desiccate.example: The desert wind desiccated the fruit.

enervate.definition: to drain of energy or vitality; to weaken
enervate.example: The long heat wave enervated the whole town.
enervate.note: Looks like "energize" but means the opposite.

sedulous.example: The sedulous researcher rechecked each figure three times.
